page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Degenerate orbitals are orbitals of the same
They differ only in the magnetic quantum
number m, that is, in their orientation.
steps.why: Orbitals of one subshell share n and l, so they share the energy as well. Only the orientation differs, and orientation costs no energy unless a magnetic or electric field is applied.
common_mistakes: Saying orbitals of the same shell are degenerate. 2s and 2p share n but have different energies.
Leaving out the words equal energy, which is the whole definition.
steps.memory_tip: Same subshell means same energy. Only the direction changes.
steps.margin_note: Name the quantum number m. It shows why the energies are equal.

steps.label: The example
lines: All three have n = 2 and l = 1, so their
The five 3d orbitals are degenerate in the
steps.why: The p subshell is the smallest clear example, with three orbitals of equal energy. Hund's rule applies to exactly this set, which is why the term is defined before that rule is stated.
common_mistakes: Giving 2s and 2p as the example. Their energies are not equal.
Giving only the name of a subshell without saying how many orbitals it holds.
steps.memory_tip: Three p orbitals, five d orbitals. Each set is degenerate within itself.
steps.margin_note: Writing n and l for the example proves the energies match.
